chapter_theme: Aravana Adigal goes on telling Manimekalai the bowl's history: the goddess Chintadevi gives Aputhiran the never-failing bowl in the Madurai rest hall; his feeding shakes Indra's seat, and when Indra comes offering a reward he laughs at a heaven where no one gives; Indra answers with rain so plentiful that no one needs the bowl, the hall falls to idlers, and Aputhiran, sailing to famine-struck Savakam, is left on empty Manipallavam, where he gives the bowl to the Gomukhi pool for some compassionate hand, starves himself to death, and is born again in Savakam to sustain its people.

cast.role: the Buddhist teacher, who tells Manimekalai the history of the bowl and its first owner
Madhavi's daughter, who now holds the bowl and hears its story
the outcast brahmin's son who feeds the poor from the rest hall in southern Madurai, the bowl's first owner
the goddess of the temple of learning in Madurai, who gives Aputhiran the bowl
Indra, king of the gods, the thousand-eyed
travellers worn by the road who come to the rest hall hungry on a night of rain
the rakes, profligates and idlers who take over the empty rest hall
the men of a ship from Savakam who tell Aputhiran of its famine and leave him on Manipallavam

manimekalai:14:1-15.reading: Aravana Adigal tells Manimekalai how, on a night of heavy rain, road-worn travellers came to the rest hall where Aputhiran slept and begged him to ease their hunger, and he, who had no food but what he begged, grieved at finding no means, until the goddess Chintadevi of the temple of learning appeared and bade him take a bowl that would not run dry though the land did, whose food would fail only as the hands of the takers tired.
manimekalai:14:1-15.nuance: The gift answers Aputhiran's grief at being unable to feed others (8, ஆற்றுவது காணான்), not his own hunger; the goddess's words at 13 to 15 are repeated almost exactly by Deepatilakai when Manimekalai receives the bowl (11:49-50), so the bowl carries the same warrant from its first owner to its second.
manimekalai:14:1-15.event: Hungry travellers beg Aputhiran for food on a rainy night; Chintadevi appears and offers him an inexhaustible bowl.

manimekalai:14:16-35.reading: The goddess puts the bowl in his hand; he praises her as the undying lamp of the temple of learning, queen of the gods and first of those on earth, feeds the travellers, and from that day feeds every creature until men, beasts and birds crowd round him with a noise like birds in a fruiting tree, so that his deeds shake Indra's white throne and Indra comes before him as a bent old brahmin with a staff, names himself, and bids him take the fruit of his great giving.
manimekalai:14:16-35.nuance: Indra's seat is shaken not by austerity but by feeding (28 to 29), and the god comes disguised as a brahmin to the man whom brahmins had driven out (kaathai 13); the offer of a reward for giving (35) sets up the refusal that follows.
manimekalai:14:16-35.event: Aputhiran takes the bowl, praises the goddess and feeds all creatures; Indra's throne trembles and Indra comes in a brahmin's form to offer him the reward of his giving.

manimekalai:14:36-48.unit_note: Boundary moved from 47 to 48: Aputhiran's question to Indra closes with தேவர்கோன்? என்றலும் at 48; the core unit cut it off before its last line.
manimekalai:14:36-48.reading: Aputhiran laughs till his ribs ache, says 'Go', and asks the king of a heaven where deeds done here are only enjoyed, where there is no one who does dharma, protects others, does good austerity or strives to cut attachment, what he could give here: food, clothes, women or attendants, to one whose divine bowl takes away the hunger of all who come and brightens their faces.
manimekalai:14:36-48.nuance: The scorn is precise: heaven is a place for consuming merit, not for making it, so a reward there would end the giving that earned it. 'வெள்ளை மகன் போல்' (36) is read as 'like a simpleton', laughing without restraint before a god.
manimekalai:14:36-48.event: Aputhiran laughs at Indra's offer and asks what a god of heaven could give him.

claims.claim: heaven is where deeds done on earth are only enjoyed, and no one there does dharma, austerity or strives to cut attachment
one who can feed all who come has nothing to gain from heaven's rewards

manimekalai:14:49-64.unit_note: Boundaries moved from 48 to 49 at the start and from 63 to 64 at the end: Indra's wish opens at 49, and the account of the idle hall ends with முறைமையது ஆக at 64, before Aputhiran leaves it at 65.
manimekalai:14:49-64.reading: Indra wills that the protector's bowl, still brimming with food, should sit idle for want of beggars, and that the whole land should overflow with plenty from spreading rain; so for Aputhiran's sake the thousand-eyed gives the world great abundance, the Pandya land that had lost its rain for twelve years grows rich and knows no hunger, and the hall's noise of eating falls silent, left to rakes, idlers and wayfarers who laugh, play dice and gamble there.
manimekalai:14:49-64.nuance: Indra's answer is a reward in form and a defeat in fact: plenty does not refute Aputhiran's scorn of heaven but takes away the hunger on which his giving depends. The sense of வசித் தொழில் (57) and whether the twelve-year drought (55 to 56) ended with this rain or preceded it are not certain; the same twelve-year formula returns for Savakam's famine at 25:101-102.
manimekalai:14:49-64.event: Indra sends abundant rain so that no one needs Aputhiran's food, and the rest hall falls silent and becomes a haunt of gamblers and idlers.

manimekalai:14:65-78.unit_note: Boundary moved from 64 to 65: line 64 closes the description of the idle hall, and Aputhiran's departure begins with ஆபுத்திரன் at 65.
manimekalai:14:65-78.reading: Aputhiran leaves the hall and goes from town to town asking for anyone who will eat, mocked by all with 'who is this?', alone like a rich man whose fortune the sea has taken, until men from a ship bow to him and tell him that in Savakam the rain has failed and creatures are dying, and he resolves to carry there the bowl that, by the king of the gods' command, has found no eaters and grown old unused.
manimekalai:14:65-78.nuance: The giver is now the beggar of beggars, asking for someone to take food; குமரி மூத்த (77), 'grown old a maiden', pictures the bowl as a girl who never married for want of a taker.
manimekalai:14:65-78.event: Aputhiran wanders finding no one to feed; shipmen tell him of famine in Savakam, and he decides to go there with the bowl.

manimekalai:14:79-94.reading: He sails gladly with the shipmen, but a gale drives the ship to Manipallavam, where he goes ashore; the crew, thinking he has re-embarked, sail off in the dark, and alone on the uninhabited island he says he will not use the great bowl that sustains all lives to sustain his own, that he has suffered lone sorrow where his merit ran out, and with folded hands lets it go into the Gomukhi pool, bidding it rise one day each year and enter the hands of any who wear compassion and dharma and sustain lives.
manimekalai:14:79-94.nuance: The bowl is refused to its owner because it is for others; Aputhiran's release sets a condition (93 to 94) that Deepatilakai later applies to Manimekalai. தவம் தீர் மருங்கின் (89) is read as the exhausting of his merit, which he gives as the cause of his plight; the unit does not say whether the work agrees.
manimekalai:14:79-94.event: Stranded on Manipallavam by the departing ship, Aputhiran consigns the bowl to the Gomukhi pool for a compassionate owner.

claims.claim: a vessel that sustains all lives must not be used to sustain the life of the one who holds it
his lone suffering comes where his merit is exhausted
the bowl should pass only to those who wear compassion and dharma and sustain lives

manimekalai:14:95-104.reading: As Aputhiran was giving up his life by the vow of not eating, Aravana Adigal went to him and asked what had befallen him, heard his many troubles, and saw him, like the sun that rises in the east, clears the dark and sets in the west, leave his body on Manipallavam with an unquenched purpose of sustaining lives, and be born from a cow's womb to rule Savakam.
manimekalai:14:95-104.nuance: The narrator is himself a witness: he was on the island at the death (96 to 98). The birth is shaped by the purpose held at death (102), and he is born in the very land whose famine he had set out to relieve. How சாவகம் ஆளும் தலைத் தாள் வேந்தன் (103) attaches to ஆ வயிற்று உதித்தனன் is not clear; kaathai 15 (15:15-30) confirms the birth from a cow, and 25:64-76 says the childless king took him up.
manimekalai:14:95-104.event: Aputhiran dies by fasting on Manipallavam, watched by Aravana Adigal, and is reborn from a cow in Savakam.

claims.claim: one who dies holding the purpose of sustaining lives is born again where that purpose can be carried out

links.note: Kural 225 ranks the strength to bear hunger below the strength to remove it; Aputhiran, who lives on begged food, grieves not at his own hunger but at finding no means to remove the travellers', and it is then that the goddess gives him the bowl.
links.teaches: Together they show the couplet's higher strength given to a man with no wealth at all: the epic makes the power to end others' hunger a gift answering grief, not a store of means, which the couplet's comparison of two strengths leaves unexamined.

gains.a: a rule that explains why the goddess answers his grief at not feeding others rather than his own need
gains.b: a case where the higher strength is wanted by one who has only the lower, so the couplet's ranking becomes a longing rather than a description of the rich

links.note: Kural 25 makes Indra the witness to the power of one who has quenched the five senses; in the epic Indra's throne trembles at a beggar's feeding of all creatures, and he comes in person to reward it.
links.teaches: The epic moves the test that brings Indra down from the ascetic's restraint to a giver's feeding, and then shows the witness turning rival, since the god's reward will undo the giving it acknowledges.

gains.a: the known Tamil rule that Indra's disturbance testifies to a human's power, so the shaken throne reads as a verdict on Aputhiran
gains.b: a story in which Indra's witness is followed by Indra's interference, which the couplet's bare 'witness enough' does not foresee

links.note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; offered heaven's reward, Aputhiran laughs that heaven is a place where no one does dharma or gives, and asks what its king could give him.
links.teaches: The couplet's hypothetical, giving is good even without heaven, becomes in Aputhiran's mouth a judgment that heaven is worse than earth for a giver, because there is no hunger there for giving to meet.

gains.a: a statement of the principle on which his laughter rests, that giving is valued apart from any reward
gains.b: an argument the couplet does not make: heaven is not merely unnecessary to giving but excludes it

links.note: Kural 19 says that if the sky gives no rain, neither giving nor austerity will last; Indra's abundant rain leaves Aputhiran's bowl idle for want of takers, and the hall of giving becomes a gambling den.
links.teaches: Rain is the condition of giving in the couplet, but the epic shows that rain in full measure can end giving too, since giving needs someone in want, so plenty sustains the giver's means and destroys his occasion.

gains.a: the Kural's rule that giving depends on rain, against which Indra's rain reads as a pointed reversal
gains.b: the other limit of its rule: too much of what makes giving possible makes it pointless

links.note: Puram 173 praises Pannan's house, where the noise of eating (ஊணொலி அரவம்) sounds like birds in a fruiting tree, as the home of the doctor of hunger; the epic uses the fruit-tree birds for the crowd at Aputhiran's hall (26 to 27), then tells how the hall's noise of eating (ஊண் ஒலி அரவம், 60) fell silent once rain removed hunger.
links.teaches: The epic takes the Sangam praise of a patron's noisy kitchen and shows its condition: the sound that proves a giver's fame lasts only as long as others are hungry, so the doctor of hunger is unmade by a world without the disease.

gains.a: the phrase ஊண் ஒலி அரவம் is shown to be the Sangam patron's formula, so its silencing marks the end of Aputhiran as a patron of the poor
gains.b: Pannan's praise gains a counter-case in which the same sound stops, exposing that the patron's glory depends on the hunger he cures

links.note: Deepatilakai tells Manimekalai that in a famine Indra's rain brought plenty and saved the brahmin about to eat dog's flesh; here Indra's rain, sent as a retort to Aputhiran, leaves his bowl idle and his hall to gamblers.
links.teaches: The epic gives Indra's rain two faces, the mercy that ends a famine and the spite that ends a giver's work, and in both tellings sets the human hand that feeds above the god's plenty, which Deepatilakai's praise alone does not show.

links.note: Kural 230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even death is sweet when giving is out of reach; alone on an uninhabited island with no one to feed, Aputhiran will not keep his own life with the bowl, gives it away and starves himself to death.
links.teaches: The epic takes the couplet's hyperbole literally: a giver cut off from anyone to give to chooses death, and refuses even the means of life that giving had put in his hands.

gains.a: a general rule that turns his fast from despair into a judgment on a life without giving
gains.b: a case where the couplet's ranking is acted on, together with the refusal to turn a giving-vessel to one's own use, which the couplet does not state

links.note: Aputhiran lets the bowl go into the Gomukhi pool to rise one day a year into the hands of one who wears compassion and dharma; in kaathai 11 it rises from Gomukhi into Manimekalai's hands as she circles the pool with Deepatilakai.
links.teaches: The receiving scene is the fulfilment of a test set by the bowl's first owner, so the bowl's coming to Manimekalai is a verdict on her compassion as well as a gift.

links.note: Aputhiran dies on Manipallavam with the purpose of sustaining lives and is born in Savakam, where he had meant to carry the bowl against a famine; in kaathai 25 the minister tells the king that before his birth Savakam lost its rain for twelve years, and that since he was born the sky has not failed and no creature has known hunger.
links.teaches: The famine Aputhiran set out to relieve with the bowl is ended by his birth instead, so the purpose held at death is fulfilled by what he becomes rather than by what he carries.

links.note: Both epics use one formula for death by fasting: Kavunthi 'gave up her life by the vow of not eating' (உண்ணா நோன்போ டுயிர்பதிப் பெயர்த்ததும், 27:83) asking whether the couple's deeds had struck at her too; Aputhiran dies by the same vow (உண்ணா நோன்போடு உயிர் பதிப் பெயர்ப்புழி, 95).
links.teaches: The twin epics give the same fasting death opposite fruits: Kavunthi's ends a life overtaken by others' karma in grief, while Aputhiran's is a passage to a birth in which his purpose of feeding goes on.

new_concepts.gloss: the vow of not eating: giving up life by fasting
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own words: உண்ணா நோன்போடு (95)

source_issues: Line 1 opens with a quotation mark (') that is not closed in this kaathai: Aravana Adigal's narration runs on from kaathai 13 and into kaathai 15 (which opens 'இன்னும் கேளாய்').
Lines 103-104 (சாவகம் ஆளும் தலைத் தாள் வேந்தன் / ஆ வயிற்று உதித்தனன்) are hard to construe; தலைத் தாள் is obscure, and the kaathai ends on the closing particle என் that runs into kaathai 15.
Line 57 வசித் தொழில் is a rare expression; read here as the work of rain.
